word:hebrew:H1007.explanation: Beth-Aven is a place in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H1212.explanation: Betsalel is a personal name, rendered Bezaleel in English.

word:hebrew:H1335.explanation: Bether means a section, part, or piece.

word:hebrew:H1340.explanation: Bath-Shua is a personal name. Here it identifies the daughter of Ammiel.

word:hebrew:H1379.explanation: Gabal means to set bounds. It can also mean to border something.

word:hebrew:H1397.explanation: Geber means a man or person.

word:hebrew:H1403.explanation: Gabriel is the name of an archangel. He is addressed as the one to make a man understand a vision.

word:hebrew:H1551.explanation: This word refers to Galilee, the name of a region in the Old Testament. It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action or quality. The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages naming or referring to Galilee in Joshua, Kings, Chronicles, and Isaiah. Its use includes references to the region as a place connected with Israel’s tribal lands and with events involving its rulers and inhabitants.

word:hebrew:H1638.explanation: Gāras means to crush or break.

word:hebrew:H1674.explanation: De’agah means anxiety, a heaviness that weighs on the heart.

word:hebrew:H1757.explanation: Dura is a place in Babylonia.

word:hebrew:H1919.explanation: Hadassah is a personal name, rendered “Hadassah.” In the Hebrew Bible, this word appears once, at Esther 2:7, so its ordinary use is as a specific name rather than a frequently repeated description or action. The available wording does not establish an additional English meaning beyond the name itself. Its significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, while the word’s lexical role is simply to identify Hadassah.

word:hebrew:H1955.explanation: Hoshaiah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action or quality. It is rendered “Hoshaiah” in all three of its Old Testament occurrences, appearing once in Nehemiah and twice in Jeremiah. The name belongs to named individuals who appear in historical settings, including passages involving speech and people being identified in relation to others. Its precise significance in each passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

word:hebrew:H2015.explanation: Haphak means to turn about or over. It can also describe a change, as when the waters were turned to blood.

word:hebrew:H2059.explanation: Vashni is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 6:28. “Vashni” is the only supported rendering, and no explicit definition is given for the name. The word’s recorded use does not establish an additional ordinary meaning beyond identifying this person.

word:hebrew:H2060.explanation: Vashti is the name of a queen.

word:hebrew:H2121.explanation: Zeidon means boiling water or a wave, and here it describes waters called proud.

word:hebrew:H219.explanation: Orah means light or luminousness. It can also name a bright plant or herb.

word:hebrew:H220.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “cotes,” referring to enclosed places associated with keeping animals. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 32:28. As a noun, it identifies a place rather than an action, quality, or person. Since the verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the surrounding context, but its ordinary lexical sense is a designated place called a cote.

word:hebrew:H2323.explanation: This Hebrew word means “new.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying something as new rather than naming an object or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Ezra 6:4. The available English rendering is consistently “new,” making that the clearest ordinary sense. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself contributes the idea of newness to whatever noun it describes.

word:hebrew:H2442.explanation: Chakah means to wait or tarry. It can also mean to long for something.

word:hebrew:H255.explanation: This Hebrew word means “doleful,” describing something sorrowful or mournful. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 13:21. In ordinary sentence use, it functions as a descriptive word rather than naming an action. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be explained further from the word record alone.

word:hebrew:H2576.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a named place, rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. Its precise English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Joshua 21:32, so it is a rare name preserved in a single passage. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there, but the word itself functions as a place designation. [p03:word:hebrew:H2576:identity] [p03:word:hebrew:H2576:occurrences]

word:hebrew:H2727.explanation: Charag means to leap suddenly and, by implication, to be dismayed or afraid.

word:hebrew:H2785.explanation: This Hebrew word means “kernels,” naming the individual parts of something rather than an action, quality, or person. It is a concrete noun used once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 6:4. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact contextual force cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains a specific tangible item identified as kernels, and the reference confirms that this is its sole recorded Old Testament occurrence.

word:hebrew:H2929.explanation: Talmon is the name of a temple doorkeeper.

word:hebrew:H2965.explanation: This Hebrew word means “off,” expressing removal or separation in a sentence. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 8:11, so its normal biblical use is represented by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of contexts. The word functions as a brief expression attached to an action or situation involving something being off. Its precise force in Genesis 8:11 depends on the verse’s surrounding wording.

word:hebrew:H3034.explanation: Yadah means to praise or give thanks in worship directed to Yahweh. It can also mean to confess.

word:hebrew:H3078.explanation: Jehojakin is the name of a Jewish king, rendered Jehoiachin in the biblical text.

word:hebrew:H3092.explanation: Jehoshaphat is a personal name used for Israelites. The name is borne by a recorder and by a king of Judah.

word:hebrew:H3117.explanation: Yom means a day, whether the daylight hours or the full day marked by evening and morning. It can also describe a defined period of time, including a span of seven days.

word:hebrew:H3243.explanation: Yanaq means to suck or nurse. It can also describe giving milk to a child.

word:hebrew:H3306.explanation: This Hebrew verb describes an action associated with a person’s inner self and appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 4:31. Its precise English meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information alone. In that occurrence, it is connected with the soul and with expressions involving a voice and a hand, showing that it describes an action or expression rather than a person or object. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its exact force there.

word:hebrew:H332.explanation: Atar means to close up or shut.

word:hebrew:H3391.explanation: Yerach means a month. It can also refer to the moon.

word:hebrew:H3409.explanation: Yarek means thigh, the fleshy part of the upper leg.

word:hebrew:H3430.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name rather than a general action, quality, or object. It refers to a named individual in the Old Testament and appears three times within 2 Samuel 21:16. The available material identifies it with the phrase יִשְׁבּוֹ בְּנֹב, but does not provide an English definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain the name’s literal components. Its precise role in that passage depends on the full context.

word:hebrew:H3445.explanation: Yeshach means hunger. It can also mean casting down.

word:hebrew:H3513.explanation: Kabad means to be heavy or weighty. It can also describe being rich. It may express giving honor to someone. It can also mean making a burden heavy.

word:hebrew:H3683.explanation: Kasach means to cut off or cut down.

word:hebrew:H3702.explanation: Kesaph means silver. It can also mean money.

word:hebrew:H3863.explanation: Lûw is a conditional word meaning “if,” and it can also express a wish.

word:hebrew:H394.explanation: Akzari means terrible. It can also describe a cruel person.

word:hebrew:H3966.explanation: Me'od means very, greatly, or exceedingly, intensifying the degree of what is being said.

word:hebrew:H4013.explanation: Mibtsar means a fortification, stronghold, or fortified city.

word:hebrew:H4109.explanation: Mahălâk means a walk or journey. It can also refer to a passage or distance.

word:hebrew:H4130.explanation: This Hebrew word means “kindred.” It identifies people connected to someone through family relationship and functions as a noun referring to that relationship or group of people. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ruth 3:2, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated occurrences. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is family connection.

word:hebrew:H4145.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “foundations,” the supporting base on which something rests or is established. It functions as a term for a firm underlying support rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament, once in Isaiah 30:32 and once in Ezekiel 41:8. Its use in these passages points to something grounded, stable, and structurally supporting. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:hebrew:H4202.explanation: Mazon means food. It can also refer to meat or other provisions.

word:hebrew:H4383.explanation: Mikshol means a stumbling-block or obstacle.

word:hebrew:H4534.explanation: Mesukah means a hedge. It can specifically describe a thorn hedge.

word:hebrew:H4578.explanation: Me'eh means the bowels or inner abdomen. It can also refer figuratively to the heart.

word:hebrew:H4592.explanation: Me'at means a little, referring to a small amount. It can also mean few, referring to a small number.

word:hebrew:H4606.explanation: This Hebrew word expresses “going,” describing movement or departure rather than naming a person or object. It functions as an action word in its one occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 6:14. Because a fuller lexical definition and the verse text are not available here, the safest understanding is its basic verbal idea: going. Its precise force in Daniel 6:14 depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:hebrew:H462.explanation: Elienai is a personal name, used to identify an individual rather than describe an action, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Bible, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:20, and is rendered “Elienai.” The available wording does not provide a separate ordinary-word definition or explain the name’s underlying sense. Its role is therefore primarily identifying: it distinguishes this person from others named in the surrounding record. The passage context would be needed to say more about the individual or the name’s significance.

word:hebrew:H4691.explanation: Metsuqah means trouble, especially distress or anguish.

word:hebrew:H4743.explanation: Maqaq means to melt or dissolve. It can describe wasting away. It can also describe being consumed away.

word:hebrew:H4831.explanation: Maralah is a Hebrew proper name rendered “Maralah,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word translated into English. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Joshua 19:11. Because it appears as a named term, its meaning for readers is chiefly its identification of Maralah itself; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there. This word is therefore best understood as a distinct biblical name, not as a general action, quality, or object.

word:hebrew:H488.explanation: Alman means forsaken or discarded, describing one cast off.

word:hebrew:H5047.explanation: Nagad means to flow, with the idea of clearing a way, like a stream issuing forth.

word:hebrew:H5090.explanation: Nâhag means to drive, lead, or carry away.

word:hebrew:H5146.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Noah.” It identifies the man who appears prominently in Genesis and is also mentioned later in Isaiah, 1 Chronicles, and Ezekiel. The name is used for Noah himself and in possessive form for something belonging to him. Within the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 46 times, mostly in Genesis. Its uses are connected with Noah’s family, God’s commands involving him, and the account of his death.

word:hebrew:H5252.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to something involved in the speech recorded in 2 Chronicles 10:15. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its ordinary meaning cannot be established confidently from repeated usage. The available scriptural evidence places it as the object of speech-related actions, but does not provide an explicit definition or English rendering. Its precise sense therefore depends on the verse’s wording and surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H53.explanation: Abishalom is a personal name, rendered Absalom in English; Absalom is identified as a son of David.

word:hebrew:H5339.explanation: Nitstsân means a blossom or flower.

word:hebrew:H5375.explanation: Nasa means to lift. It can also describe bearing a punishment or carrying something. It may also refer to forgiving a wrong.

word:hebrew:H5425.explanation: Nathar describes leaping or being violently moved. It can also mean letting loose or undoing.

word:hebrew:H5450.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “burdens”—loads or oppressive demands placed upon people. It is used six times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in Exodus, where it consistently concerns the burdens carried or imposed upon Israel. In Exodus 6:6, the word appears in God’s declaration that he would bring Israel out from under those burdens, linking the term with his promised action to deliver and rescue his people. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

policy.futureRepairGate: Reopen only after a verified source-alignment, lexical-identity, or evidence-view correction materially changes the closed evidence.
policy.priorReviewerNotes: The lexical definition supports “roundness,” but the supplied Song 7:3 evidence and translations concern breasts and do not directly support that sense. The claim therefore lacks valid Scripture support.

word:hebrew:H5487.explanation: Soof means to come to an end. It can also describe something being consumed or fulfilled.

word:hebrew:H5533.explanation: Çakan means to endanger. It can also mean to impoverish, or make poor.

word:hebrew:H5641.explanation: Sathar means to hide or conceal, literally or figuratively. It can describe someone being hidden from view, or something kept secret rather than revealed.

word:hebrew:H5704.explanation: Ad marks a limit or extent—“as far as” in space and “until” in time. It can mark a time endpoint, as when someone returns to the ground, or the endpoint of a stated distance.

word:hebrew:H5748.explanation: Ugav means a reed instrument of music. In these passages, it is rendered as an organ.

word:hebrew:H581.explanation: Innûn means “they,” referring to more than one. It can also be rendered “these,” as when it points to the kingdoms in view.

word:hebrew:H5836.explanation: Ezri is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H5968.explanation: ʻAlaph means to veil or cover. Figuratively, it can describe becoming faint or languid.

word:hebrew:H5982.explanation: This Hebrew word means “pillars,” referring to upright structural elements. It is a noun used for individual supports as well as groups of supports, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle, temple, and other buildings. The word occurs 112 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent reference to pillars as physical parts of constructed spaces. Its surrounding context determines the particular building or arrangement intended.

word:hebrew:H6019.explanation: Amram is a personal name. Amram is identified as Kohath’s son and the father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.

word:hebrew:H6020.explanation: “Amramites” is a plural noun naming a group of people identified with Amram. It functions as a family or lineage designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers and 1 Chronicles, and is rendered “Amramites” in each recorded translation alignment. The word therefore points to people belonging to the Amramite group, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific setting in which they are mentioned.

word:hebrew:H6055.explanation: “Ananiah” is a personal name used in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears twice, both times in Nehemiah, at Nehemiah 3:23 and 11:32. The available wording preserves it as “Ananiah,” so its ordinary role is to identify a person, not to describe an action, quality, or object. Because no explicit definition is given, the safest explanation is that this word functions as a personal name.

word:hebrew:H6132.explanation: Aqar means to pluck up by the roots.

word:hebrew:H6473.explanation: Paar means to open wide. It can also describe gaping with the mouth.

word:hebrew:H6518.explanation: Paraz means a chieftain, but this occurrence is rendered as villages.

word:hebrew:H6554.explanation: Parpar is a river of Syria, one of the rivers of Damascus.

word:hebrew:H673.explanation: This Hebrew word identifies a person by regional or family association, rendered “Ephraimite” or “Ephrathite.” It functions as a descriptive noun or designation rather than naming an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs five times, describing people connected with places or groups bearing these related names. The surrounding verse determines which geographical or familial association is intended, but the central idea is a person identified as Ephraimite or Ephrathite.

word:hebrew:H6781.explanation: Tsamid means a bracelet or arm-clasp. It can also mean a covering over an open vessel.

word:hebrew:H6907.explanation: Qubbaʻath means a goblet or deep bowl.

word:hebrew:H7131.explanation: Qareb means near. It can also describe approaching or drawing near, including priests coming near to Yahweh to minister.

word:hebrew:H718.explanation: Aru means “behold” or “lo,” drawing attention to what follows.

word:hebrew:H7272.explanation: Regel means a foot, the part used in walking.

word:hebrew:H7298.explanation: Rahat means a channel or watering trough.

word:hebrew:H7337.explanation: Rachab means to broaden or enlarge. It can describe making room, as Yahweh makes room. It can also describe opening wide, as with a mouth.

word:hebrew:H7395.explanation: Rakkab means a charioteer, or driver of a chariot.

word:hebrew:H7463.explanation: Re'eh means a male companion or friend.

word:hebrew:H754.explanation: This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “lengthening,” referring to making something longer or allowing it to continue for a greater period. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel. As a word with this meaning, its precise sense in either verse depends on what is being lengthened and the surrounding sentence. The available occurrences are Daniel 4:27 and Daniel 7:12, but the verse text is needed to explain the specific force in each passage.

word:hebrew:H7566.explanation: Resheph is a personal name for an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H7661.explanation: Shabats means entanglement or, figuratively, perplexity; it can also describe anguish that takes hold.

word:hebrew:H7728.explanation: Shôwbêb means apostate, heathenish, or heathen; it is rendered “backsliding” in the phrase “backsliding daughter.”

word:hebrew:H7764.explanation: “Shuni” is a personal name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, and English renderings preserve it as “Shuni.” The name itself is presented without an explicit definition, so it should be understood as a proper name rather than a translatable description. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding family and genealogical context.

word:hebrew:H7809.explanation: Shachad means to bribe. It can also mean to give a reward.

word:hebrew:H7830.explanation: Shachats means haughtiness, an attitude of pride. It can also refer to a lion.

word:hebrew:H7845.explanation: Shachath means a pit. It can also refer figuratively to destruction.

word:hebrew:H8127.explanation: Shen means a tooth. It can also refer figuratively to a crag.

word:hebrew:H8242.explanation: Saq means coarse cloth or sackcloth used in mourning. It can also mean a bag or sack.

word:hebrew:H835.explanation: Esher expresses happiness. It describes a person as happy and can also describe people as blessed.

word:hebrew:H8376.explanation: Ta'a means to mark out or designate—to point something out.

word:hebrew:H840.explanation: Asareel is a personal name preserved in the Hebrew Old Testament, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the genealogy recorded at 1 Chronicles 4:16. The available wording does not provide a broader lexical definition or explain the name’s etymology, so its safest ordinary meaning is simply the person’s name, rendered “Asareel.” It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament.

word:hebrew:H8426.explanation: Todah means thanksgiving, as an expression of thanks. It can also describe confession. It may also refer to a thanksgiving offering.

word:hebrew:H8615.explanation: Tiqvah means hope or expectation. It can also mean a cord used as an attachment.

word:hebrew:H8659.explanation: Tarshish names a place on the Mediterranean. It can also refer to a merchant vessel associated with that port. It is also a personal name, including that of a prince of Persia and Media.

word:hebrew:H8660.explanation: Tirshatha is a title for a Persian deputy or governor.

word:hebrew:H879.explanation: The Hebrew word refers to a place named “Beer.” It functions as a proper place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in Isaiah 15:8. The available wording supports “Beer” as the word’s meaning, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the place’s specific role in that passage.

word:hebrew:H897.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. The available material does not provide a direct gloss or approved meaning term, so no more specific definition can be stated responsibly here. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezekiel 25:7, but the verse text is not included. A precise understanding therefore requires reading that passage in context.

word:hebrew:H912.explanation: Bedeiah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Bedeiah.” It identifies one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:35. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s identity can be stated, but no further detail about the person or the passage should be inferred from the name alone.
